q: 1. Pick up the correct sequence of geological cycle for the formation of soil
explain: The geological cycle of soil formation consists of weathering of parent rock, transportation of particles, deposition in a new location, and eventual upheaval.

q: 2. Which of the following is a glacial soil?
options: Deposited at the bottom of the lakes
explain: Glacial soils are transported and deposited directly by glacier ice, which none of the other options (river, lake, sea) describe.

q: 3. 'Drift' is the material picked up, mixed, disintegrated, transported and re-deposited by
explain: Drift refers to all material transported and deposited by glaciers, either directly by moving ice or by the meltwater (glacier water) flowing from it.

q: 4. Talus is the soil transported by .............
explain: Talus is scree that accumulates at the base of a slope or cliff due to gravity-driven rockfall.

q: 5. The soil transported by flowing water is called
explain: Soil carried and deposited by rivers/streams (flowing water) is termed alluvial soil.

q: 6. Shape of clay particles is .............
explain: Clay minerals commonly form flaky or needle-like (acicular) particle shapes due to their sheet-silicate crystal structure.

q: 7. Chemical weathering of soil is caused due to
explain: Chemical weathering of parent rock into soil occurs through multiple processes — oxidation, carbonation, and hydration — all contributing to mineral breakdown.

q: 8. Chemical weathering occurs because of .............
explain: Oxidation, carbonation, and hydration are all chemical processes that break down rock minerals, contributing to chemical weathering.

q: 9. Pile foundation are suitable for
explain: Piles are primarily used to transfer structural loads down through weak upper soil layers to a firm, competent bearing stratum below (end-bearing piles).

q: 10. Agent responsible for the transportation of soil is
explain: Soil transportation and deposition can occur via wind (aeolian), water (alluvial/lacustrine/marine), or gravity (talus/colluvial) — all are recognized transporting agents.

q: 11. The soil transported by running water is called .............
explain: Soil transported and deposited by flowing rivers/streams is classified as alluvial soil.

q: 12. Caissons are structures used for
options: Dewatering while laying foundations in proper position
explain: Caissons are large prefabricated box/well structures sunk into the ground/water to allow foundations to be constructed properly in position, especially below water or through soft strata.

q: 13. The soil transported by wind is called .............
explain: Wind-transported and deposited soil is termed aeolian soil (e.g., loess, dune sand).

q: 14. Generally hand augers are used when the depth is about .............
explain: Hand augers are a simple manual tool practical only for shallow exploration, typically up to about 6 m depth.

q: 15. Lacustrine soils are those soils which are .............
options: deposited at the bottom of the lakes
explain: Lacustrine soils are, by definition, transported by water and deposited at the bottom of lakes.

q: 16. Shallow footing is one whose depth is
explain: Per Terzaghi's definition, a shallow foundation has depth less than or equal to (approximately) its width, not strictly less than, more than, or always equal — hence 'none of the above' as per the book's answer.

q: 17. Mode of transportation for alluvial soils is generally
explain: By definition, alluvial soils are those transported and deposited by the action of flowing water (rivers/streams).

q: 18. Generally soil refers to .............
explain: Per the reference key soil is described as a solid medium, referring to its mineral solid framework.

q: 19. Bore holes are found to be economical than the test pits when the depth of exploration is around .............
explain: Beyond about 6 m depth, boring becomes more economical than excavating open test pits, which get costly and unstable at greater depth.

q: 20. A raft foundation is preferred for .............
options: load bearing walls of multistoreyed buildings
columns of a building which are closely spaced
explain: When columns are closely spaced (individual footings would overlap), a raft foundation combines them into one continuous slab.

q: 21. Chemical weathering of soil is caused due to .............
explain: Chemical weathering results from oxidation, hydration, carbonation, and leaching acting together on rock minerals.

q: 22. The soil transported by glaciers either by ice or water is called .............
explain: Glacial deposits, whether carried by ice or glacial meltwater, are collectively termed drift.

q: 23. Mechanical weathering of soils is caused by .............
explain: Mechanical (physical) weathering results from temperature cycling, water action, and ice wedging combined.

q: 24. Honey combed structure is found in .............
explain: Honeycomb structure, formed by arching of bulky grains bridging over pore spaces, is characteristic of coarse sands (and fine sands/silts under certain deposition).

q: 25. Soil transported by water and deposited at the bottom of the lake is known as .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'loess'; by standard definition, soil deposited at the bottom of a lake is actually called lacustrine soil, and loess is wind-deposited.

q: 26. Who coined the term soil mechanics?
explain: Karl Terzaghi, considered the father of soil mechanics, coined the term and founded the discipline.

q: 27. Cohesionless soils are formed due to .............
options: leaching action of water on rocks
blowing of hot and cold wind
explain: Cohesionless (granular) soils like sand and gravel form mainly through physical (mechanical) disintegration of parent rock.

q: 28. When the particles of soil are oriented 'edge to edge' or 'edge to face' with respect to one another, the soil is said to have .............
explain: Edge-to-edge or edge-to-face particle orientation, common in clay deposition, produces a loose, open flocculent structure.

q: 29. Peat is nothing but .............
explain: Per the reference key, peat is classified here as organic clay, reflecting its high organic decomposed plant matter content.
